---
title: "A paired transfer-learning experiment"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{A paired transfer-learning experiment}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

The unit of comparison is a target database, prediction problem, feature profile,
training budget, and repetition. All five methods predict the same held-out
patients. Source models and source development populations stay fixed while the
target training budget changes.

Freeze the target and outcome cohort definitions, population settings, observation
windows, database locations, and phenotype definitions before running.
Snapshot identifiers are optional. Named cohort tables are reused when present
and generated when absent. Existing tables must contain the intended complete
cohorts; use new tables for revised definitions and new output folders for changed data.
The first implementation supports one index per patient and binary outcomes.
A phenotype's complete definition must use information available at prediction
time; checking its cohort start date alone is insufficient.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(TransferLearning)
curve <- createLearningCurveSettings(
  trainingEvents = c(25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 500, 1000, Inf),
  repetitions = 10, folds = 5, testFraction = .25
)
# See inst/examples/config.R for the complete configuration and registry contract.
results <- runExperiment(settings, databaseRegistry)
plotLearningCurves(results, "logLoss")
plotTransferEffects(results, "logLoss")
```

Within each training subsample, normalization is estimated separately in each
inner training fold. Validation patients never contribute normalization factors
or model fitting. The actual validation assignments remain in the runner. Each
prepared training subset is passed directly to `fitPlp()` with a local all-ones
fold table, which disables internal tuning and CV predictions without altering
PLP model settings. This does not use `createDefaultSplitSetting(nfold = 1)`.
Prior variances are selected by pooled validation log loss,
then the final model is fitted using all sampled training patients. A boundary
optimum triggers one three-decade grid extension and is still flagged if it remains
on the resulting boundary. No test metric is used for choosing variances.

`priorCoefs` implements penalized corrections around source slopes; it is not
warm starting an ordinary target-only lasso. The target intercept is free. To
preserve the source linear predictor under multiplicative normalization, transfer
slopes are converted by semantic covariate ID using the ratio of target to source
normalization maxima. Source-only features retain their source scale and slope.
Neither intercept positions nor autogenerated matrix column names identify
predictors.

The aggregate `differences.csv` contains paired improvements (positive favors
transfer) for AUROC, AUPRC, log loss, and Brier score. `intervals.csv` contains
paired test-patient bootstrap intervals for AUROC and log loss. These intervals
condition on fitted models. Repeated training samples describe a different source
of variability and share the same test patients. Present database/problem-specific
curves and heterogeneity rather than treating all repeated predictions as
independent observations.

Patient splits, predictions, saved models, normalization factors, tuning losses,
warnings, and skipped/failed job reasons remain in the local results directory.
Resume requires the same manifest and immutable data snapshots. A failed job is
retried; a completed job is reused. After an interrupted process, verify it has
stopped before removing a stale `.runner-lock` directory.

PLP JSON model persistence remains subject to numerical rounding. Reloaded source
models for unfinished jobs may therefore differ slightly from in-memory models.
The correctness patch and runner-side tuning do not resolve exact restart
equivalence; no precision sidecar is added.

Event budgets count outcome-positive patients in the sampled target training set.
Controls follow the development pool’s ratio, rounded to the nearest whole patient.
This gives exact event counts and nested samples while keeping a fixed test set.
PLP recommends `trainEvents`, but its learning-curve helper converts events into
fractions; this runner enforces counts directly. Event-based capacity is useful
across prevalences, but does not make performance or statistical power prevalence-independent.
Plots default to training events; `abscissa = "patients"` uses total training size.
